title: Earth from Above
description: Watch the globe turn, peer into a hurricane and learn how scientists read the planet from a distance.

questions.prompt: The white patterns crossing Earth's surface in this time-lapse are mainly what?
questions.hint: These patterns belong to the atmosphere, not the solid ground.
questions.explanation: The white patterns are clouds, seen above the oceans and continents as Earth turns.

media.alt: A time-lapse view of the turning Earth.
media.description: Silent time-lapse: pale swirling patterns cross the land and oceans of a turning globe. The animation plays at 3,600 times real speed; its timer shows elapsed hours and minutes.
media.credit: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio / Horace Mitchell, Galileo imagery, visualization 1375.

questions.prompt: In an ordinary colour photograph of Earth from space, the broad blue areas are mainly what?
questions.hint: Think about what covers most of the planet's surface.
questions.explanation: The blue areas are mainly ocean water, which covers roughly 71 percent of Earth's surface.

media.alt: A blue globe with clouds, a tapering continent near its center and a bright white continent below.

questions.prompt: What is the relatively calm central region shown in this hurricane photograph called?
questions.hint: It is surrounded by a ring of much taller storm clouds.
questions.explanation: The eye is the storm's central region; the surrounding eyewall contains intense convection and strong winds.

questions.prompt: Why can a satellite take a thermal-infrared image of the ground at night?

choices.text: Infrared detectors illuminate the whole planet
Night air becomes transparent to visible light

questions.hint: A surface does not stop giving off heat when the Sun sets.
questions.explanation: Thermal sensors detect emitted radiation, so they do not depend on reflected sunlight.

questions.prompt: Which orbital arrangement lets a weather satellite appear fixed above one point on the equator?

choices.text: Any low orbit passing over both poles
A circular orbit completed every 90 minutes
A circular equatorial orbit matching Earth's rotation

questions.hint: Its motion must keep pace with the ground beneath it.
questions.explanation: A geostationary satellite orbits eastward above the equator once per sidereal day.

questions.prompt: The clouds move during this sequence, but the continental coastlines retain their relative positions. Why is tectonic drift not visible?

choices.text: Tectonic plates only move at night
Plate movement is far too slow over about a day
The ocean prevents continents from moving

questions.hint: Compare a day's motion with the centimetres plates typically move in a year.
questions.explanation: Plate motions measured in centimetres per year are negligible in a time-lapse covering about 25 hours.

questions.prompt: Why does a geostationary weather satellite have a poor view of regions near Earth's poles?

choices.text: Polar regions emit no electromagnetic radiation
Earth's curvature places them near or beyond its horizon
Polar ice blocks radio waves everywhere
The satellite orbits behind the Moon at noon

questions.hint: The satellite stays above the equator instead of passing overhead at high latitudes.
questions.explanation: From an equatorial geostationary orbit, high latitudes are viewed at very oblique angles and the poles are beyond the horizon.

questions.prompt: A satellite image renders vigorous vegetation bright red. What does that most likely mean?

choices.text: Near-infrared measurements were assigned to the red display channel
The plants have all turned red in visible light
The sensor recorded only surface temperature
The image contains no measurement data

questions.hint: Display colours can stand for wavelengths our eyes cannot see.
questions.explanation: False-colour composites often map near-infrared reflectance to red; healthy vegetation reflects strongly in that band.

questions.prompt: In a mature hurricane, which feature surrounds this eye and typically contains the strongest sustained surface winds?

choices.text: The centre of the clear opening

questions.hint: Focus on the steep ring just outside the opening.
questions.explanation: The eyewall is the convective ring around the eye and normally contains the storm's strongest sustained winds.

questions.prompt: Which sensor is an active remote-sensing instrument?

choices.text: A radiometer measuring emitted terrestrial infrared
A detector measuring naturally emitted microwave energy
A radar that transmits pulses and measures their echoes

questions.hint: An active sensor supplies the energy used to probe its target.
questions.explanation: Radar sends out electromagnetic pulses and records the return; passive sensors receive naturally available radiation.

questions.prompt: A band has 30-metre square ground pixels. Ignoring edge effects, about how many pixels cover one square kilometre?
questions.hint: Work with areas: each pixel covers 30 times 30 square metres.
questions.explanation: One square kilometre is 1,000,000 square metres; dividing by 900 gives about 1,111 pixels.

questions.prompt: Away from the equator and surface friction, steady geostrophic wind reflects an approximate balance between which two effects?

choices.text: Gravity and centrifugal force about the Sun

questions.hint: It is the balance that allows wind to run roughly along straight isobars.
questions.explanation: In geostrophic balance, the horizontal pressure-gradient force is balanced by the Coriolis force.

questions.prompt: In the ideal Northern Hemisphere Ekman model, a steady wind blows due north over deep open water. In which direction is the depth-integrated wind-driven transport?
questions.hint: The integrated transport differs from the direction of the very top layer.
questions.explanation: Ideal Ekman transport is 90 degrees to the right of the wind in the Northern Hemisphere. Right of north is east.
